 The 57 th Meeting of the GST Council was held today in New Delhi, under the chairpersonship of the Union Finance & Corporate Affairs Minister Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman. 


 


 The participants included Chief Ministers of Delhi, Goa, Haryana, Jammu & Kashmir, Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra, and Meghalaya; Deputy Chief Ministers of Manipur and Telangana; the Finance Ministers and senior members of States/Union Territories with Legislative Assembly, Secretary, Department of Revenue; Chairman and Members of Central Board of Indirect Taxes & Customs and senior officials of the Ministry of Finance. 


 


 


 Next-Gen reforms made as per recommendations of the GST Council in its 56 th meeting last year had focussed on rate rationalisation and reduction of rates. In the 57 th meeting today, GST Council made recommendations relating to process reforms primarily covering registration, returns, refund and adjudication; clarifications regarding applicability of GST on supply of certain goods and services; and other measures for trade facilitation and streamlining compliances in GST. FAQs are being issued for clarification of doubts. Major recommendations made in the 57 th GST Council meeting are as below: 


 A. Process Reforms 


 A1. Registration related reforms 


 1. Streamlining registration process with clear guidelines on filing and processing 


 1.1 As per recommendations of GST Council made in 56 th meeting, automatic registrations, without officer intervention, are being granted by the portal under rule 14A of the CGST Rules, 2017, in cases where the applicant does not intend to pass on ITC more than ₹2.5 lakh per month. To streamline processing of registration applications in remaining cases, the GST Council made the following recommendations in the 57 th meeting: 


 
 issuance of a comprehensive circular specifying the documents and information required for GST registration, along with frequently asked questions (FAQs), to simplify the filing and processing of registration applications . 

 amendment in the registration application in FORM GST REG-01, to provide for drop boxes for selection of prescribed documents/information, so that both the taxpayer and the tax officer have clarity regarding the documents/information to be furnished. 

 The GST portal to provide user-friendly interface, for filing registration application with clear navigational paths, drop-down lists, tool-tips and contextual guidance to facilitate correct filing of such applications. 

 

 1.2 This will reduce rejections and queries raised in respect of registration applications on account of lack of correct information/details and will expedite processing of registration applications by the tax officers. 


 2. Rationalization of Procedure for Amendment in GST registration : 


 2.1 The GST Council recommended an amendment to rule 19 of the CGST Rules, 2017, to provide for automatic acceptance of amendments to all registration particulars on the portal, except those relating to the Principal Place of Business (PPoB). Further, for taxpayers registered under rule 14A of the CGST Rules, 2017 (automatic route), amendments of all registration particulars, including those relating to the PPoB, will be accepted automatically on the portal. 


 2.2 This will facilitate easy and almost real time updation of registration details on the portal in such cases, without interface with the tax officers. 


 3. Rationalization of registration cancellation process under GST: 


 3.1 The GST Council recommended amendments in the CGST Act, 2017 and the CGST Rules, 2017, to simplify the registration cancellation process, as follows: 


 3.1.1 Automatic cancellation of registration on the application of the taxpayer 


 Phase 1: The applications for cancellation of registration in FORM GST REG-16 will be accepted automatically by the system, once all pending returns are filed and all dues are paid, in the following cases: 


 
 where the taxpayer has not passed on ITC exceeding ₹2.5 lakh in any of the months since registration; 

 where the taxpayer has passed on ITC exceeding ₹2.5 lakh in a month, but has filed the final return in FORM GSTR-10 within specified time period. 

 

 Phase 2: All the applications for cancellation of registration will be accepted automatically by the system, once all pending returns are filed and all dues are paid. FORM GST REG-16 will be amended so that the details of FORM GSTR-10 can be furnished in the said application itself. 


 3.1.2 Suo-moto cancellation of registration 


 
 Amendment in rule 21 of the CGST Rules, 2017, to omit certain grounds of cancellation of registration by the tax officers. 

 Amendment in rule 21A and rule 22 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and insertion of rule 23A in CGST Rules, 2017, to provide for a mechanism of system based cancellation and revocation of registration based on non-compliance and subsequent compliance of the defaults of non-filing return or non-furnishing of the details of the bank account, within specified time period. 

 

 3.2 These measures will simplify and expedite the process of cancellation of registration and will reduce officer interface and bring more transparency to the cancellation process. 


 4. Simplified GST registration mechanism for small sellers on the Electronic Commerce Operators (ECO) platform :

 Six-year plan to make India self-reliant in pulses by 2030-31 


 


 From Import Dependence to Self-Sufficiency 


 India is the world's largest producer of pulses, a globally important, protein-rich food crop. Pulses contain 20-25% protein , more than double that of wheat and nearly three times that of rice. Pulses contribute significantly to India's agricultural exports and remain a vital part of Indian diets, ensuring nutritional security . Recognising this importance, the government launched the 'Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses' on October 11, 2025. As the nation observes the first anniversary of the Mission’s launch on October 11, this landmark initiative continues its momentum, backed by a financial allocation of ₹11,440 crore spanning 2025–26 to 2030–31. The Mission seeks to achieve self-sufficiency in pulses production. It focuses on boosting domestic production, reducing import dependence, and enhancing farmers' income through a comprehensive value-chain approach. 


 A Mission with a Clear Target 


 Under the Mission, by 2030-31, production is expected to reach nearly 350 lakh tonnes , with yield rising to 1,130 kg per hectare . Key strategic measures driving these targets include : 


 
 Focus on enhancing production of Tur, Urad and Masoor 

 Promotion of climate-resilient seeds and improved seed quality 

 Distribution of 87.5 lakh free seed kits and 126 lakh quintals of certified seeds over six years 

 Expands pulse cultivation area by 35 lakh hectares to reach a total targeted area of 310 lakh hectares by 2030–31. 

 Cluster-based approach covering 489 districts to intensify production 

 Establishment of 1,000 processing units (dal mills) 

 Assured procurement of Tur, Urad and Masoor via NCCF and NAFED from willing and registered farmer. 

 Expected to reduce import dependence and conserve foreign exchange 

 

 India’s Pulse Powerhouse 


 India’s pulse sector showed strong growth in domestic production, farming area, and crop yield during 2025-26. Steady agricultural progress and strong local output continue to strengthen the nation’s pulse economy. 


 
 India’s total pulse production rose to 274.09 lakh tonnes in 2025-26 ( 3 rd Advance Estimates ) from 256.83 lakh tonnes in 2024-25. 

 India's pulse cultivation area expanded significantly from 277.20 lakh hectares in 2024-25 to 286.46 lakh hectares in 2025-26 . 

 The major regions of Pulse cultivation are Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Jharkhand, Odisha and West Bengal. 

 National pulse productivity improved as the overall yield increased from 926 kg per hectare in 2024-25 to 957 kg per hectare in 2025-26 . 

 

 


 
 India’s pulses imports declined by 31.52% , from ₹ 46,427.60 crore in 2024 - 25 to ₹ 31,793.59 crore in 2025 - 26 . 

 India’s pulses exports rose 13.40% , from USD 855 million in 2024-25 to USD 969.53 million in 2025-26 . The total export volume reached a total volume of 10.01 lakh tonnes during 2025–26. 

 In 2025-26, major export destinations included China, UAE, Bangladesh, the U.S.A., and Sri Lanka . 

 

 Rising MSP, Assured Procurement 


 The government continues to strengthen price security for pulse farmers through substantial increases in Minimum Support Prices. Higher support prices ensure fair returns and incentivize increased domestic production of key pulse crops. 


 
 For the marketing season 2024-25 , the Minimum Support Price (MSP) for Urad was fixed at ₹ 7,400 per quintal, which was increased by ₹ 800 ( 10.81% ) to ₹ 8,200 per quintal for 2026-27 . 

 For the year 2024-25 , the MSP for Tur ( Arhar ) stood at ₹ 7,550 per quintal, which saw an enhancement of ₹ 900 ( 11.92% ) to reach ₹ 8,450 per quintal in 2026-27 . 

 For the year 2024-25 , the MSP for Masur ( Lentil ) was set at ₹ 6,700 per quintal, which was revised upward by ₹ 300 ( 4.48% ) to ₹ 7,000 per quintal for 2026-27 . 

 

 


 Under the Mission, National Cooperative Consumers' Federation of India Limited (NCCF) and National Agricultural Cooperative Marketing Federation of India Limited (NAFED) are authorized to procure 100% of Tur, Masur, and Urad for a period of four years (2025–26 to 2028–29). As of June 17, 2026, key achievements from the NCCF Pulses Procurement Dashboard include: 


 
 NCCF achieved a total pulses procurement of 10.55 lakh tonnes across 9 states. A total Minimum Support Price (MSP) value of ₹ 7,047 crore was released directly to farmers. The initiative successfully benefited 4.69 lakh farmers out of 7.74 lakh total registered farmers. 

 

 
 Under Kharif 2025-26 , 7.89 lakh tonnes of pulses worth ₹ 6,431 crore were procured, benefiting 3.66 lakh farmers . 

 Under Rabi 2026-27 , procurement of pulses reached 23.51 lakh tonnes with an MSP release of ₹ 14,217 crore , benefiting 10.20 lakh farmers . 

 

 
 Pulses procurement expanded from 18,39,504.77 tonnes in 2024-25 to 31,40,883.92 tonnes in 2025-26 . 

 

 Mission’s Key Early Progress 


 The Mission's early progress reflects steady momentum in building infrastructure and expanding farmer support. Key achievements so far include: 


 
 The Mission envisages 1,000 pulse processing units , with 528 units already allocated to States and Union Territories in the first phase .

 TRAI today has released the “Indian Telecom Services Performance Indicator Report” for the quarter ending 30 th June 2026. This Report provides a broad perspective of the Telecom Services in India and presents the key parameters and growth trends of the Telecom Services as well as Cable TV, DTH & Radio Broadcasting services in India for the period covering 1 st April 2026 to 30 th June 2026 compiled mainly on the basis of information furnished by the Service Providers. 


 Executive Summary of the Report is enclosed. The complete Report is available on TRAI’s website ( www.trai.gov.in and under the link http://www.trai.gov.in/release-publication/reports/performance-indicators-reports ). For any suggestion or any clarification pertaining to this report, Shri Vijay Kumar, Advisor (F&EA) , TRAI may be contacted on Tel. +91- 20907773 and e-mail: fea1-div@trai.gov.in . 


 The Indian Telecom Services Performance Indicators 


 April–June 2026 


 Executive Summary 


 
 Total number of Internet subscribers increased from 1092.79 million at the end of March 2026 to 1114.17 million at the end of June 2026, registering a quarterly rate of growth of 96%. Out of 1114.17 million Internet subscribers, number of Wired Internet subscribers are 47.73 million and number of Wireless Internet subscribers are 1066.43 million. 

 

 Composition of Internet Subscription 


 


 
 The Internet subscriber base is comprised of Broadband Internet subscriber base of 1087.50 million and Narrowband Internet subscriber base of 26.67 million. 

 The broadband Internet subscriber base increased by 2.03% from 1065.88 million at the end of March 2026 to 1087.50 million at the end of June 2026. The narrowband Internet subscriber base decreased by 0.89% from 26.91 million at the end of March 2026 to 26.67 million at the end of June 2026. 

 Wireline subscribers decreased from 48.25 million at the end of March 2026 to 47.82 million at the end of June 2026 with a quarterly rate of decline 0.88%. On Y-O-Y basis, wireline subscriptions increased by 0.71% at the end of quarter ending June 2026. 

 Wireline Tele-density decreased from 3.38% at the end of March 2026 to 3.35% at the end of June 2026 with quarterly rate of decline 1.06%. 

 Monthly Average Revenue per User (ARPU) for wireless service increased by 1.19%, from ₹184.91 in quarter ending March 2026 to ₹187.12 in quarter ending June 2026. On Y-O-Y basis, monthly ARPU for wireless service increased by 3.11% in this quarter. 

 The ARPU per month for the pre-paid segment is ₹200.72 and the ARPU per month for the post-paid segment is ₹114.26 for quarter ending June 2026. 

 On an all-India average, the overall MOU per month decreased by 2.65% from 959 in quarter ending March 2026 to 933 in quarter ending June 2026. 

 Prepaid MOU per subscriber is 1055 and Postpaid MOU per subscriber per month is 279 in quarter ending June 2026. 

 Average revenue realization per GB for wireless data usage decreased from ₹7.51 in quarter ending March 2026 to ₹7.13 in quarter ending June 2026 with quarterly rate of decline of 5.07%. 

 Number of wireless (Mobile) data subscribers has increased from 1026.75 million at the end of March 2026 to 1045.55 million at the end of June 2026 with quarterly rate of growth of 1.86%. Further, total volume of wireless (mobile) data usage also increased from 77,953 PB during quarter ending March 2026 to 84,424 PB during quarter ending June 2026 with growth of 8.30%. 

 Average Wireless (Mobile) Data Usage per wireless data subscriber per month increased from 26.70 GB during quarter ending March 2026 to 28.39 GB during June 2026 with quarterly rate of growth 6.32%. 

 Gross Revenue (GR), Applicable Gross Revenue (ApGR) and Adjusted Gross Revenue (AGR) of Telecom Service Sector for the quarter ending June 2026 has been ₹1,06,797 Crore, ₹101,036 crore and ₹88,796 Crore respectively. GR increased by 1.60%, ApGR by 2.43% and AGR increased by 2.40% in the quarter ending June 2025, as compared to previous quarter. 

 The Y-O-Y rate of growth in GR, ApGR and AGR in the quarter ending June 2026 over the same quarter in last year have been 10.50%, 9.52% and 9.19% respectively. 

 Pass Through Charges decreased from ₹12,494 Crore in the quarter ending March 2026 to ₹12,241 Crore in the quarter ending June 2026 with quarterly rate of decline of 2.02%. The Y-O-Y rate of growth 17.06% has been recorded in pass-through charges in the quarter ending June 2026. 

 The License Fee increased from ₹6,936 Crore in the quarter ending March 2026 to ₹7,103 Crore in the quarter ending June 2026. The quarterly and the Y-O-Y rates of growth in license fees are 2.41% and 9.18% respectively in this quarter. 

 

 Service-wise composition of Adjusted Gross Revenue 


 


 
 Access services contributed 83.85% of the total Adjusted Gross Revenue of telecom services. In Access services, Gross Revenue (GR), Applicable Gross Revenue (ApGR), Adjusted Gross Revenue (AGR), License Fee, Spectrum Usage Charges (SUC) and Pass Through Charges increased by 1.43%, 2.86%, 2.72%, 2.73%, 2.83% and -8.83% respectively in the quarter ending June 2026.

 Introduction 


 Introduced on 1 July 2017, GST brought many Central and State taxes into a common framework. It marked a milestone in India’s reform journey. It gave effect to the principle of “ One Nation, One Tax” and helped move India towards an integrated tax system. 


 Over the past nine years, standardised procedures and rationalised rates have supported greater transparency, accountability and economic growth. They have also strengthened the vision of ‘Ek Bharat - Shreshtha Bharat’. 


 Building on this progress, the 56th GST Council recommended Next-Generation reforms to simplify the four-tier GST rate structure . The new structure has two main rates , 5% and 18%, and a special 40% rate for select goods and services. 


 This reform process has continued at the 57th meeting in October 2026. T he Council recommended further process reforms, clarifications on selected goods and services, and measures to facilitate trade and streamline compliance. 


 
 
 
 
 GST in Numbers: Wider Reach, Scale and Collections 


 A wider taxpayer base: Registered taxpayers increased from around 60 lakh in 2017 to ~1.70 crore as of September 2026. 


 A large-scale digital tax system: As on 30 September 2026, the GST System had cumulatively processed 3,053 crore invoice uploads and 833.82 crore e-way bills. 


 Strong revenue growth: Gross GST collections reached ~₹12.46 lakh crore during April-September 2026 , registering an increase of 11.6% Y-o-Y. 

 
 

 
 

 


 


 


 Making GST Registration Simpler, Faster and More Predictable 


 
 The proposals of the GST Council seek to create a more predictable and taxpayer-friendly GST registration framework. They are intended to support smoother business operations and encourage wider participation in the formal economy. 


 Reforms in the Registration process: 




 The GST Council recommended the following: 


 
 A comprehensive and detailed documentation along with FAQs will be issued for processing registration applications. 

 The registration application will be amended to simplify the filing process and improve clarity for taxpayers and tax officers. 

 The GST portal will provide a user-friendly interface for filing registration applications, with clear navigational paths, drop-down lists, tool-tips and contextual guidance. 

 

 
 
 
 
 What is Input Tax Credit? 


 It is the credit a registered person can claim for tax on goods or services received. 


 For eg: If a manufacturer has paid tax of ₹10,000 on raw material purchase and collected tax of ₹25,000 on product sales. Consequently, the net tax payment amount is ₹15,000 and the manufacturer can claim the tax paid on raw material. 

 
 

 
 

 


 These measures would facilitate correct filing of registration applications and reduce rejections and queries raised in respect of such applications. 


 These measures would facilitate correct filing of registration applications and reduce rejections and queries raised in respect of such applications. 


 


 


 
 Automatic Acceptance 




 For easy and near real-time updation, the Council suggests automatic acceptance of amendments to registration particulars. This would be enabled on the portal, except for changes relating to the Principal Place of Business (PPoB). 


 
 
 
 
 What is Principal Place of Business? 


 Section 2(89) of the CGST Act, 2017 defines it as follows: "principal place of business" means the place of business specified as the principal place of business in the certificate of registration”. 

 
 

 
 

 


 For taxpayers registered through the automatic route, amendments to all registration particulars, including PPoB, would be accepted automatically. 


 
 Registration Cancellation Process 




 To simplify the registration cancellation process, the Council recommended amendments in the CGST Act, 2017 and the CGST Rules, 2017. The proposal includes 


 
 Automatic cancellation : To reduce the officer’s interface the Council proposed the reforms in phased manner. 

 

 
 
 
 
 Phase 1 

 
 

 
 
 The cancellation applications would be accepted automatically after pending returns are filed and all dues are paid. 


 
 This would apply to taxpayers who have not passed on ITC exceeding ₹2.5 lakh in any month . 

 It would also apply where ITC exceeded ₹2.5 lakh in a month , if the final return is filed within the specified time. 

 
 
 

 
 
 Phase 2 

 
 

 
 
 All the applications for cancellation of registration will be accepted automatically by the system, once all pending returns are filed and all dues are paid. FORM GST REG-16 will be amended so that the details of FORM GSTR-10 can be furnished in the said application itself. 

 
 

 
 

 
 Suo-moto cancellation: To expedite the process of cancellation certain grounds for cancellation of registration by tax officers would be removed, reducing intervention. 

 

 


 

 A system-based mechanism would enable cancellation and revocation based on non-compliance and subsequent compliance . The mechanism covers defaults relating to non-filing of returns or non-furnishing of bank account details within the specified time. 


 


 
 
 
 
 Reform for E-commerce sellers 


 The reforms suggested by the GST Council provide a simplified registration mechanism for small taxpayers making supply through E-commerce platforms . 


 Small sellers passing ITC not more than ₹2.5 lakh/month (excluding stock transfer) can opt for simple registration (PAN based) in States/UTs other than their Home State/UTs. 


 The electronic commerce operator (ECO) warehouse can be declared as the PPoB in a State/UT where there is no physical presence. 


 This would facilitate ease of doing business for small e-commerce sellers by enabling them to establish their businesses in other States.

He also said that the Reserve Bank of India had once again raised its growth projections for the current year and expressed confidence that India would continue to grow at over 7 per cent and remain the fastest-growing large economy.

 The National SC-ST Hub (NSSH) is advancing inclusive entrepreneurship by enabling SC/ST enterprises to build capabilities and access wider market opportunities. Through interventions spanning finance, technology, training, mentoring and market linkages, the scheme addresses key barriers across the enterprise journey. Its focus on public procurement further connects SC/ST-owned MSEs with institutional buyers. With growing beneficiary reach, training support and procurement participation, NSSH is helping create a more competitive MSME ecosystem. 

 

 
 

 
 

 Building an Inclusive Entrepreneurship Ecosystem 


 Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) provide an important pathway to entrepreneurship, employment and economic opportunity across India’s urban and rural areas. Making these opportunities more inclusive requires enabling entrepreneurs from historically underrepresented communities to participate, compete and grow. In this context, promoting enterprise ownership among Scheduled Caste (SC) and Scheduled Tribe (ST) communities is an important priority. Greater access to finance, skills, technology and markets can help broaden their participation in India’s MSME ecosystem. 


 National SC-ST Hub: Enabling Enterprise Growth 


 Launched on 18 October 2016 , the National SC-ST Hub (NSSH) Scheme provides focused support to enterprises across different stages of their growth journey. Implemented through the National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC) , the scheme helps address barriers faced by SC/ST-owned enterprises and supports their participation in public procurement. 


 Enterprise development initiatives under NSSH include training, mentoring, business development, networking and knowledge support. Together, these interventions help entrepreneurs improve business capabilities, access new opportunities and build more competitive enterprises. 


 


 Expanding Reach, Deepening Inclusion 


 NSSH’s impact is reflected not only in the number of entrepreneurs supported, but also in their growing participation in markets. By linking entrepreneurial support with procurement opportunities, the scheme is helping SC/ST-owned businesses improve their capabilities, expand market presence and pursue sustainable growth.

Posted On:

 PM GatiShakti National Master Plan (PMGS-NMP) has evolved from a national infrastructure mapping platform into a wider planning framework. It brings together Ministries, States and infrastructure networks through a GIS-based platform to support integrated planning and project coordination. Today, it covers 58 Central Ministries and Departments and all 36 States and Union Territories. 

 
 

 
 

 Infrastructure As The Engine of Viksit Bharat 


 India is building infrastructure at a scale that requires coordination across sectors and modes of transport. Roads, railways, ports, airports, waterways and utilities often intersect across the same regions. Planning these networks together can help in cost and time savings, coordinate projects and use existing infrastructure more efficiently. This created a need for an approach that integrates different infrastructure networks into a common planning framework. 


 To address this need, the PM GatiShakti National Master Plan was launched on 13 October 2021. It brought data from different ministries, States and Union Territories onto a common Geographic Information System (GIS)-based platform. PM GatiShakti enables planners to view infrastructure, geographic features, economic zones and other relevant data together, supporting data-driven planning and decision-making for infrastructure projects. Five years on, this approach has grown into a nationwide planning framework. 


 PM GatiShakti At A Glance 


 PM GatiShakti is guided by six principles that seek to make infrastructure planning more integrated, efficient, and coordinated. This includes integrated development, multimodal infrastructure, last mile connectivity, expedited land acquisition, minimised clearances and reduced ecological impact. 


 


 Key features of PM GatiShakti include: 


 
 
 
 
 Do You Know? 

 PM Gati Shakti incorporates infrastructure schemes from various Ministries and State Governments, such as Bharatmala, Sagarmala, inland waterways, dry/land ports, and UDAN. 

 
 

 
 

 
 Seven Infrastructure Engines: Roads, Railways, Ports, Waterways, Airports, Mass Transport and Logistics Infrastructure form the core sectors of the plan. 

 Whole-of-Government Planning: The National Master Plan covers 58 Central Ministries and Departments and all 36 States and Union Territories, enabling infrastructure proposals to be planned and assessed across sectors. 

 Integrated Digital Planning: The NMP brings together infrastructure, and geospatial information on a common GIS-based platform, supporting spatial planning and decision-making. 

 Wider Data Access: The PM GatiShakti Public platform provides access to 230 approved datasets , enabling site suitability analysis, connectivity mapping, alignment planning and compliance checks. 

 

 
 Data Layers: Over 23,493 data layers, as of 12 October 2026, bring infrastructure and other relevant information onto the common GIS-based platform. 

 

 
 
 
 
 ITLA: Strengthening Integrated Transport Planning 


 Complementing PM GatiShakti, the Union Cabinet recently approved the establishment of the Integrated Transport & Logistics Authority (ITLA). The Authority will focus on long-term transport planning and coordination. 


 


 ITLA will prepare a National Transport Master Plan with a planning horizon of ten years or more. It will assess sectoral and annual transport plans, and undertake technical appraisal of projects costing ₹500 crore or more. The authority will also monitor their implementation. It will also develop a National Transport Data Repository (NTDR) by integrating information from sources such as FASTag, Vahan, and GSTN e-way bills. 

 
 

 
 

 How GatiShakti Works: From Coordination to Project Planning 


 PM GatiShakti has a three-tier institutional framework comprising the following: 


 
 Empowered Group of Secretaries (EGoS) : Chaired by the Cabinet Secretary, the EGoS oversees the implementation of PM GatiShakti and reviews, considers and approves changes in the Master Plan. 

 Network Planning Group (NPG): The NPG brings together the Heads of Network Planning Divisions from infrastructure Ministries and Departments. It examines infrastructure proposals and ensures unified planning, integration and optimisation. It also monitors developments under the National Master Plan for project planning. 

 Technical Support Unit (TSU): The TSU comprises domain and subject-matter experts who support the evaluation process. It assists the Logistics Division in performing its role as the PM GatiShakti Secretariat. 

 

 As of 11 August 2026 , the NPG had evaluated 396 infrastructure projects with a total estimated cost of about ₹18.66 lakh crore . Of these, 256 projects had been sanctioned, of which 198 were under implementation . The institutional framework is supported by a digital platform that provides planners with geospatial data, satellite imagery and analytical tools . 


 Gati Shakti Vishwavidyalaya: Building Expertise for Integrated Infrastructure Planning 


 Gati Shakti Vishwavidyalaya (GSV) is a first-of-its-kind university focused exclusively on the transport and logistics sectors. Established in 2022, the university brings together education, executive training and research across transport-related disciplines.

items.title: Khadi & Village Industries: From Tradition to Enterprise
key_lines: In 2025–26, sales of Khadi and Village Industries products reached a historic ₹1.87lakh crore, the highest level recorded (as of May 2026).
Compared with 2013–14, sales grew by 501%, while production increased by 380% to ₹1,25,296 crore.
Employment in the sector increased by 56% to 2.04 crore.
It rose from ₹4 per hank in 2013–14 to ₹15 per hank currently, an increase of approximately 275%.
Women constitute more than 80% of approximately five lakh artisans in the Khadi sector.
items.text:
Posted On:
 13 OCT 2026 11:12AM by PIB Delhi
 

 
 
 

 
 
 A charkha spinning in a village once spoke of nationalism. Today, that spirit is taking new shape through a growing ecosystem of rural enterprises. Honey, herbal products, banana fibre, textiles and other village industries are creating new possibilities for traditional skills. 


 The spirit of self-reliance continues to resonate with the vision of Vocal for Local and Atmanirbhar Bharat. Traditional skills and local resources are finding new markets through access to finance, technology and training. 


 This growing connection between local enterprise and consumers is also reflected in the Khadi Mahotsav. The Khadi Mahotsav takes place annually from 2 October to 31 October . With a particular focus on youth, the campaign sensitises them towards Khadi and “Vocal for Local” and encourages the public to buy Khadi and local products. 


 At the centre of this transformation is the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) . It is a statutory body established under the Khadi and Village Industries Commission Act, 1956. The Act mandates KVIC to plan, promote, facilitate, organise and assist village industries. It covers measures related to training, raw materials, marketing, research, and quality improvement . It also supports skill development and research, while providing technical information and facilities related to Khadi and village industries. 


 


 In 2025–26, sales of Khadi and Village Industries products reached a historic ₹1.87lakh crore, the highest level recorded (as of May 2026). Compared with 2013–14, sales grew by 501%, while production increased by 380% to ₹1,25,296 crore. Employment in the sector increased by 56% to 2.04 crore. The remuneration paid to artisans has also increased. It rose from ₹4 per hank in 2013–14 to ₹15 per hank currently, an increase of approximately 275%. 


 
 
 
 
 One hank is equivalent to 840 yards of yarn in length and one pound by weight. 

 
 

 
 

 Building Rural Businesses, One Artisan at a Time 


 From acquiring skills to accessing markets, a range of interventions is supporting artisans and village industries. 


 KVIC has a network of 35 departmental and non-departmental training centres . Training covers food products, bakery, beekeeping, agarbatti, candles, motor repairing and several other activities. During FY 2025-26, 79,682 trainees received training under various KVIC training programs. 


 Women constitute more than 80% of approximately five lakh artisans in the Khadi sector. In 2025–26, 47,382 women received training under various KVIC programmes, accounting for approximately 59% of all trainees. 


 Training is complemented by interventions including toolkit and equipment distribution, marketing support and other measures. 


 


 Since March 2008, the Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP) has provided employment opportunities to nearly 97.95 lakh people through KVIC. 


 One such beneficiary is Shri Jitendra Baitha, who established a bakery products manufacturing unit in Bihar in 2020. His venture has an annual turnover of ₹72 lakh and currently provides employment to 20 people, in the local community. 


 Support also includes enterprise finance and the tools and technology needed for production. 


 The Gramodyog Vikas Yojana empowers artisans by providing modern machines, toolkits and equipment. During 2025–26, 37,769 such machines, toolkits and equipment were distributed. KVIC, under the scheme, has distributed more than 3.23 lakh machines, toolkits and equipment (May 2026). 


 These efforts are complemented by measures that strengthen the wider ecosystem in which Khadi institutions and artisans operate. 


 The Khadi Vikas Yojana helps Khadi institutions improve products, add value and respond to changing market demand. Its Modified Market Development Assistance provides greater flexibility for value addition and market-oriented pricing. During 2024–25, ₹245 crore was disbursed to 1,097 Khadi Institutions, benefiting 1,45,484 artisans. 


 Access to affordable credit adds another layer of support. Under the Interest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate Scheme , eligible Khadi institutions can access credit at a concessional interest rate of 4% per annum. 


 For artisans, the workplace itself also matters. The Workshed Scheme provides improved production spaces and a more congenial working environment. During 2025–26, up to December 2025, 1,309 artisans benefited under the scheme. 


 These measures support artisans with improved working conditions and access to resources for production. 


 From Village Enterprises to Wider Markets 


 Across village industries, traditional skills and local resources are being developed into new businesses and products, supported by technology, training and market linkages. Research and development efforts are strengthening productivity, quality and competitiveness. 


 Shri S.P. Singh built his enterprise around honey and cookies, with support under the PMEGP scheme through KVIC . Based in Punjab, his business now provides employment to around 200 workers and exports its products to international markets. Honey and cookies are among its key products, with the United States accounting for a major share of exports. 


 After receiving support in 2010, the enterprise gradually expanded its export presence through participation in international exhibitions. KVIC facilitated participation in exhibitions across Dubai, the United States and the Middle East, helping the enterprise connect with overseas buyers. Today, the business exports to 36 countries and is developing a second unit in Rajpura, Punjab, to expand honey exports to European markets. 


 


 For Shri B. Sundaraj , a naturally fragrant plant became the foundation for a village enterprise. Through his Agarbathi Unit, he produces agarbatti, herbal products, Vetiver Agarbathi and Vetiver Sambu

 The National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) received Rs 9.68 crore from users of India's biological resources during the period from 01.04.2026 to 30.09.2026, in accordance with the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, as amended in 2023, and the ABS Regulations. Of the total receipts, Rs 9.56 crore was received towards access to biological resources from various sectors as given below. 


 Sector-wise Contributions 


 The Agri-seed sector accounted for the largest share of receipts, with Rs 7.16 crore, followed by Food & Beverages at Rs 1.59 crore and Animal Husbandry at Rs 62.01 lakh. Receipts classified under IPR-related applications amounted to Rs 11.24 lakh. Other receipts were from AYUSH, Red Sanders wood, Cosmetics and others.

 Key Contributions 


 M/s East West Seeds India Ltd was the largest ABS contributor, with around Rs 2.01 crore across multiple payments. The single largest ABS payment was Rs 1.17 crore from M/s Synergia Life Science Ltd. Other significant ABS contributions included M/s Tata Chemicals Pvt Ltd (Rs 52.06 lakh), M/s Indena India Pvt Ltd (Rs 45.89 lakh), M/s Grow Indigo Ltd (Rs 45.79 lakh), M/s Novozymes South Asia (Rs 44.11 lakh), and M/s Nongwoo Seed India (Rs 40.53 lakh). 


 M/s Nunhems India Ltd made upfront payments of around Rs 1.64 crore. Contributions were received from both domestic and international entities, including entities from Sri Lanka, Germany, France, the Republic of Korea and Bhutan. 


 Diversity of Biological Resources 


 The receipts reflect the utilisation of a diverse range of biological resources across agriculture, food, pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, medicinal plants, microorganisms and livestock. These include agricultural crops such as chickpea, red lentil, green moong, horse gram, flaxseed, guar gum, tapioca, buckwheat, brown rice, cauliflower, okra, hot pepper, brinjal and ridge gourd. 


 The biological resources also include medicinal plants such as Ashwagandha, Shatavari, Kalmegh, Vasaka, Licorice, Arjuna, Bacopa, Gotukola and Moringa, as well as soil microorganisms including Azospirillum, Azotobacter, Bacillus, Rhizobium, Trichoderma and Metarhizium. The range further includes livestock genetic resources such as Mithun (Bos frontalis), Jersey cattle (Bos taurus) and frozen semen of Murrah buffalo (Bubalus bubalis), as well as Red Sanders wood sourced from cultivated sources and auctioned material. 


 Linking Benefit Sharing with Biodiversity Conservation 


 Since 2008, the NBA has realised around Rs 278 crore through ABS and disbursed more than Rs 200 crore towards biodiversity conservation and benefits for communities, farmers, institutions and other benefit claimers across the country. 


 The ABS mechanism goes beyond monetary collection by linking the utilisation of biological resources with biodiversity conservation, sustainable use and equitable sharing of benefits. Funds disbursed through the State Biodiversity Boards and Union Territory Biodiversity Councils support conservation of biological resources, preparation and updation of People's Biodiversity Registers, strengthening of Biodiversity Management Committees, biodiversity research and documentation, and benefits to local communities and other benefit claimers. 


 The ABS mechanism provides a framework through which India is progressively translating the utilisation of its biological diversity into tangible outcomes for biodiversity conservation, sustainable use and benefit of local communities. The receipts generated during the period reflect the continued implementation of India's ABS framework and the fulfilment of benefit-sharing obligations by users of biological resources.

key_lines: Indian Railways loaded 135.35 million tonnes of freight in September 2026, compared to 127.52 million tonnes in September 2025, registering a 6.14 per cent growth over the corresponding month last year.

 Indian Railways recorded continued growth in freight and passenger segments during September 2026, with higher freight loading, and growth across several key commodity categories.  Freight Loading Registers 6.14% Growth

 Industrial pollution abatement is emerging as a key pillar river rejuvenation, with regulation increasingly evolving from conventional enforcement to continuous compliances, scientific monitoring, cleaner production, resource efficiency and technological improvement. 


 Under Namami Gange Programme, industrial pollution control has been strengthened through systematic inventorisation and annual inspection of Grossly Polluting Industries (GPIs), independent technical assessments, implementing sector-specific Charters, monitoring of Common Effluent Treatment Plants (CETPs), targeted action plans and sustained regulatory follow-up. Together, these interventions are creating a more accountable and sustainable pathway for industries to reduce pollution while improving water and resource efficiency. 


 From periodic inspection to continuous compliance 


 A major intervention has been the establishment of an Annual Inspection mechanism for GPIs, which commenced in 2017 with support of CPCB, the National Regulatory Authority. The programme focusses on 100% inspection of GPIs in the Ganga basin, through third party agencies e.g., technical institutes of national importance and online submission of inspection reports through mobile applications/web portals to enhance efficacy and transparency. For the 2026 inspection cycle, 40 technical institutes have been nominated to participate in the inspection process. 


 The scale of this monitoring framework has expanded considerably since 2017. In the 2025 inspection cycle, 3,703 GPIs were assessed (1,296 GPIs in the Ganga basin and 2,407 GPIs in the Yamuna basin). The exercise covered 113 districts across six States and one Union Territory, with the GPIs having potential to discharge into 46 tributaries and sub-tributaries of the Ganga and Yamuna. 


 The inspections go beyond visual assessment. The prescribed methodology includes studying the compliance of the industries against ‘Consent to Operate’ issued by State regulators (State Pollution Control Board) to the individual Industries, sampling from ETP inlets, outlets and aeration tanks, assessment of flow, pH, BOD, COD, TSS and TDS, verification of OCEMS connectivity, examination of recipient drains and water bodies, groundwater assessment, checks for any bypasses and ZLD profiling wherever applicable. Cases involving bypasses, multiple discharge points or defunct/non-existent/non-operational ETPs/ GPIs are reported with geo-tagged photographic or videographic evidence in the portal itself. 


 Regulation delivering measurable results 


 The progressive assessment of GPIs demonstrates the impact of sustained regulatory intervention. Across the assessed GPIs, compliance increased from 39% in 2017 to 70% in 2025, while the number of operational GPIs stood at 3,154 in 2025 increasing from 888 in 2017. During the same period, BOD load declined from 26 TPD (2017) to 12.02 TPD (2025), reflecting a substantial reduction in pollution load. 


 


 


 


 The Ganga basin has exhibited a progressive trend from 2017 to 2025, with compliance rising from 39% in 2017 to 86% in 2025. BOD load declined from 26 TPD to 7.16 TPD, representing a 72.46% reduction, while effluent discharge declined from 349 MLD to 274.88 MLD, a reduction of 21.24%. 


 


 


 


 


 


 The GPI Inspection further recorded that, among 3,145 operational GPIs, 2,715 were compliant, while non-compliant operational GPIs stood at 448, accounting for approximately 14% of operational GPIs. The regulatory process for non-compliant GPIs includes issuance of Show Cause Notices and closure action by State regulators (SPCBs), as applicable. 


 Thus, regulation is functioning not merely as an enforcement mechanism, but as a continuous self-improvement mechanism—inspection, identification, corrective action and follow-up. 


 Independent Technical Institutions: adding scientific rigour 


 A distinctive feature is the involvement of independent technical institutions in industrial inspections. The 2025 exercise engaged 25 technical institutes, while 40 institutes have been nominated for the 2026 cycle. The prescribed inspection team includes at least two experts from a technical institute, a SPCB officer alongwith the participation from State Mission for Clean Ganga/District Ganga Committees. 


 This model brings guidance from scientific and sector-specific expertise into regulatory oversight for technological or processes improvement in GPIs for pollution and resources reduction with overall improvement in efficiency and compliance to the norms. It also enables inspection findings to be supported by laboratory analysis, OCEMS verification, field observations and geo-tagged evidence, thereby strengthening the credibility and effectiveness of compliance assessment. 


 Sector-specific Charters: from pollution control to pollution prevention 


 The regulatory framework has also expanded upstream - from treating pollution after it is generated to preventing pollution at source. Sector-specific Charters have been developed for Pulp & Paper, Sugar, Distillery, Textile and Tannery sectors. These five sectors collectively represented around 70% of GPIs in the Ganga basin and 88% of the total pollution load in the earlier assessment. 


 The Charter for Water Recycling and Pollution Prevention Industries specifically seeks to optimise water and chemical use, reduce freshwater consumption and wastewater generation, improve effluent treatment and promote reuse and recycling, with the ultimate objective of preventing discharge of untreated effluent into recipient river streams.

 The Ayush services sector is emerging as an important avenue for women’s participation in the workforce, with female representation exceeding 50 per cent across several organised segments, according to a recent assessment of the sector. Women account for 43 per cent of the overall Ayush services workforce, with their representation crossing 50 per cent in hospitals, day-care centres, educational institutes and wellness establishments. 


 The Ayush services economy, covering Ayurveda, Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy, was estimated at US$36.92 billion in FY2024-25, registering a robust 16.91 per cent CAGR since FY2022-23. The sector directly supports an estimated 1.76 million livelihoods across healthcare, wellness, education and allied services. 


 


 Highlighting the employment potential of the sector, Shri Prataprao Jadhav, Union Minister of State (IC) for Ayush and Minister of State for Health & Family Welfare, reiterated, “The growing Ayush services sector is creating meaningful employment opportunities across healthcare, wellness, education and allied services. Its expansion is not only strengthening India’s healthcare ecosystem but also opening new avenues for entrepreneurship, skill development and women’s participation in the workforce.” 


 According to the Ayush Service Sector Report, a study by RIS released recently on Ayurveda Day 2026, women’s participation is particularly significant across organised Ayush establishments. Female representation exceeds 60 per cent in spas and wellness resorts, stands at 58 per cent in educational institutes, 57 per cent in day-care centres and 53 per cent in hospitals. 


 The findings highlight the growing role of women across diverse segments of the Ayush services ecosystem, including healthcare delivery, education, wellness and allied services. More than one million livelihoods are concentrated in local and standalone clinics, demonstrating the sector’s extensive employment footprint across urban and rural areas. 


 Secretary, Ministry of Ayush Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha emphasised, “The expansion of organised Ayush services, supported by quality standards, skilling, digital infrastructure and stronger institutional networks, can significantly enhance both the scale and quality of employment. Greater participation of women in organised Ayush establishments also demonstrates the sector’s potential to contribute to inclusive economic growth.” 


 Standalone clinics remain the largest revenue-generating segment, contributing an estimated US$16.21 billion, or 43.9 per cent of the sector’s revenue, while day-care centres account for another US$10.13 billion. Together, the two segments contribute more than 70 per cent of the sector’s revenue. Ayurveda remains the largest individual system, accounting for US$17.73 billion, or around 48 per cent of the total Ayush services revenue. 


 


 The wellness segment is witnessing particularly strong growth, recording a 21.29 per cent CAGR; meanwhile, Yoga centres registered around 75 per cent revenue growth over two years, reflecting rising demand for preventive health and wellness services. 


 The sector is also gaining traction in Medical Value Travel (MVT), generating an estimated US$1.77 billion in FY2024-25. International patients, though accounting for around 5 per cent of patient volumes, contribute approximately 15-25 per cent of hospital segment revenue, with therapeutic programmes typically involving stays of 5 to 11 days. 


 The assessment projects the Ayush services sector to expand from US 36.92 billion in FY 2024–25 to an estimated US 216–318 billion by 2047, with substantial potential to generate employment opportunities across diverse areas, including healthcare delivery, wellness, education, medical travel, research, digital health and allied services. 


 The growing representation of women across organised Ayush establishments, alongside the sector’s expanding economic and employment footprint, highlights its potential to contribute to women’s economic participation, inclusive growth and India’s broader development journey towards Viksit Bharat@2047.

 The Ministry of Tribal Affairs (MoTA), Government of India, convened the Second Regional Review Conference on implementation of the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (FRA) at Kolkata, West Bengal on 9 th October 2026. The Conference brought together senior functionaries of the Tribal Welfare, Revenue and Forest Departments and Tribal Research Institutes of eight States, namely West Bengal, Assam, Tripura, Jharkhand, Odisha, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh. Additionally senior officials of Andhra Pradesh were invited to share the best practices the State has undertaken on digitization, integration of FRA titles into government records and taking up proactive measures on convergence of livelihood schemes with FRA titleholders and providing credit facilities to the right holders. Further, District officials- Collectors, Sub Collectors and ITDP/ITDA Project Officers, where districts having a large pendency of FRA claims, also attended, to review the status of implementation and deliberate on a coordinated way forward. The Conference follows the First Regional Review Conference held in Bengaluru on 10 September 2026 for the Southern States. 


 


 Proceedings began with a Welcome Address by the Principal Secretary, Tribal Development Department, Government of West Bengal, who apprised the gathering of the objectives of the Conference and extended a formal welcome to the dignitaries and delegates which was followed by the Keynote Address of the Joint Secretary, MoTA, and the Special Address of the Secretary, MoTA. 


 In his Keynote Address, the Joint Secretary said that as on 31 st August 2026, over 54 lakh claims had been received nationally, and about 25 lakh titles had been distributed. About 11 lakh claims still remain pending at different stages, while over 18 lakh claims have been rejected. He noted that Madhya Pradesh, Odisha and Assam account for substantial pendency concentrated in particular districts. He highlighted that the Regional Conference focuses on the following key priorities such as timely disposal of pending claims and review of rejected claims in accordance with the Act and Rules, reconciliation of FRA data, digitization of FRA case records, incorporation of recognised rights into revenue and forest records, accelerate recognition of Community Forest Resource Rights and Habitat Rights recognition for PVTGs. 


 In her Special Address, the Secretary, MoTA, said that the FRA places the rights, dignity and aspirations of forest-dwelling communities at the heart of inclusive and sustainable development. She appreciated the experience of Andhra Pradesh in digitization and creating of record of rights of FRA title holders to avail the post claim support, Odisha and Chhattisgarh in pioneering the recognition of PVTG habitat rights and recognition of highest number of IFR claims. She stressed that recognition of Community Forest Resource Rights (CFRR) must be matched by the capacity to exercise them. Gram Sabhas need support to prepare and implement Community Forest Resource Management Plans, and States should operationalise the joint advisory of MoTA and the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. This advisory enables integration of these plans with the working and management plans of Forest Departments, while keeping the authority of the Gram Sabha central. She added that assistance is available under DA-JGUA for capacity building of Gram Sabha for preparation of such CFR management plans and their execution. She also called for PVTG-wise roadmaps for Habitat Rights which need to be prepared with sensitivity and the active participation of traditional institutions and the Gram Sabhas of all concerned villages. She further emphasised that recognised rights must be incorporated into Revenue and Forest records with accurate maps, and that convergence with programmes for productive land use, housing and livelihoods must become a regular part of implementation. 


 The Director, FRA, MoTA, presented the national scenario, including pendency in high-pendency States and priority districts. Her presentation also covered the importance of incorporating the Record of Forest Rights into revenue and forest records in line with the Ministry’s advisory of 24 June 2026 and Habitat Rights under the Ministry’s guidelines of 5 January 2026. She also outlined the financial support available from MoTA to take forward such interventions by the States. Further, states were also asked to reconcile data discrepancies and delays in Monthly Progress Reports. Also, States have been directed to prepare an action plan for strengthening Gram Sabhas to create awareness of FRA rights, post Claims support, and for preparation of the CFR management plan on priority. The Deputy Secretary, TRI & IT, MoTA, spoke on digitisation of FRA records and demonstrated the National-level FRA Portal and the FRA mobile app which can be useful to advance digitization, geospatial integration and decision-support systems for FRA governance. Also, urged the States to integrate their existing FRA records through Application Programming Interface (API). 


 


 State-wise Presentations 


 Officers of the eight States presented the status of FRA implementation in their respective States, covering claim pendency, incorporation of records, Community Forest Resource Rights and Habitat rights of PVTGs and digitisation of FRA records. The States also presented the action plan for timely disposal of pending claims, review of rejected claims, recognition of CFRR and habitat rights in a time bound manner and strengthening convergence so that eligible right-holders receive livelihood and development support. 


 The Conference concluded with a Valedictory Address by the Joint Secretary, MoTA, and a Vote of Thanks by the Director, FRA, MoTA.

items.title: Strong Statistical Systems Key to Achieving Viksit Bharat @ 2047: Dr. P. K. Mishra
items.text:
Posted On:
 13 OCT 2026 12:40PM by PIB Delhi
 

 
 
 

 
 
 Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister, Dr. P. K. Mishra, today delivered the keynote address at the inaugural session of the Conference of State Planning, Finance and IT Secretaries, organised by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) in New Delhi. Emphasising the importance of credible statistics, data harmonisation and technology-enabled governance, he said a strong statistical system is essential for evidence-based policymaking and achieving the vision of Viksit Bharat @ 2047. 


 Dr. Mishra said statistics, data, technology, planning and governance are increasingly interconnected elements of India’s development journey. A robust statistical system, he noted, must enable governments to measure development progress across States and districts, assess policy outcomes, identify gaps and ensure that public resources deliver the intended results. “What cannot be measured cannot be managed effectively. And what cannot be managed effectively cannot be transformed sustainably,” he observed. 


 Highlighting the need to modernise economic measurement, Dr. Mishra said India’s statistical systems must evolve alongside an economy that is increasingly digital, formalised and interconnected. He noted that the introduction of the new National Accounts Series, with 2022-23 as the base year, alongside updated Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Index of Industrial Production (IIP) series, represents an important step towards keeping statistical methodologies aligned with changing economic realities. 


 Underscoring the importance of State Statistical Systems, Dr. Mishra said India’s development story is fundamentally a story of its States, where policies are implemented, economic activity takes place and citizens experience development outcomes. He called for stronger institutional capacity and closer Centre–State coordination to improve the quality of official statistics. 


 Dr. Mishra said artificial intelligence, machine learning, geospatial systems, satellite imagery and advanced analytics offer significant opportunities to improve the timeliness, accuracy and usefulness of official statistics. However, he cautioned that technological advancement must remain guided by statistical quality, transparency, privacy, security and accountability. “Speed cannot come at the cost of accuracy. Greater use of data cannot come at the cost of confidentiality,” he said. 


 Dr. Mishra described statistics as an important instrument of cooperative federalism, enabling States and the Centre to compare outcomes, identify best practices and learn from regional differences. As India progresses towards 2047, he said, national averages alone would not suffice; granular data at State, district and local levels would be increasingly necessary to identify development gaps and guide interventions. 


 Concluding, Dr. Mishra called for a collective national effort involving MoSPI, State Statistical Offices, Finance, Planning and IT Departments, NITI Aayog, academic institutions and other stakeholders. He said India needs a statistical architecture that is trusted, transparent, technology-enabled, interoperable and policy-relevant. Such a system, he added, would not merely measure India’s transformation but also help guide and accelerate it towards Viksit Bharat @ 2047. 


 ***

 A high-level inter-ministerial review meeting was held today at Krishi Bhawan, New Delhi, to implement crop residue (stubble) management in mission mode during the ongoing paddy harvesting season. The meeting was co-chaired by Union Minister for Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare, and Rural Development Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan, and Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Shri Bhupender Yadav. Union Minister of State for Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare, Shri Bhagirath Choudhary, the agriculture ministers of key states, including Delhi-NCR, Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, Union Agriculture Secretary Shri Atish Chandra, Union Secretary for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Shri Narendra Bhushan, and other senior officials from the Central and state governments were present at the meeting. 


 During the meeting, both Union Ministers made it clear that very little time remained between the completion of crop harvesting and the sowing of rabi crops. Therefore, the administrative machinery must move beyond files and take action directly on the ground on a war footing. They issued firm directions for district-level collectors to convene meetings promptly, strengthen monitoring and ensure that practical solutions were implemented without delay. The emphasis was on swift coordination and effective action at the field level to prevent stubble burning during the critical period. 


 


 “Stubble is not a problem, but a means of improving farmers’ income and soil health”: Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan 


 Addressing the meeting, Union Agriculture Minister Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan said that paddy harvesting was underway and farmers were eager to prepare their fields for the next crop. In such circumstances, merely telling farmers not to burn stubble would not be enough. They must be provided with alternatives that are easy to use, readily accessible and affordable. Stubble burning not only causes air pollution but also destroys beneficial soil organisms and burns away essential nutrients, turning them into ash. It is therefore necessary to protect Mother Earth and preserve soil health. When crop residue is incorporated into the soil, it can be converted into organic manure; when removed from the field, it can serve as a source of additional income for farmers through its use in bio-CNG, bio-ethanol, electricity generation and animal fodder. 


 He further stated that the objective was not merely to prevent stubble fires but to develop a robust system in which farmers would have no need to burn crop residue in the first place. The aim should be to create practical and economically viable arrangements for managing stubble while enabling farmers to benefit from opportunities such as carbon credits through environmentally sustainable agricultural practices. Such an approach would protect the environment while also strengthening farmers’ livelihoods and improving the long-term sustainability of agriculture. 


 Concern over rising incidents in Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan; directions issued for action on a war footing 


 Commenting on the analysis of the data presented during the meeting, Shri Shivraj Chouhan said it was encouraging that, between September 15 and October 12, stubble-burning incidents had declined significantly compared with the corresponding period last year. Haryana recorded a reduction of 53.3 per cent, while Uttar Pradesh registered a decline of approximately 32 per cent. Punjab had also recorded some reduction. However, expressing concern over the increase in stubble-burning incidents in Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, the Union Agriculture Minister directed both states to identify the affected districts and villages and immediately implement special action plans to address the situation. He emphasised that a substantial portion of harvesting was still pending. Therefore, even states that had achieved a reduction in incidents must not become complacent and should maintain complete vigilance throughout the remaining harvesting period.

Posted On:
 13 OCT 2026 4:48PM by PIB Delhi
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 India's fight against tuberculosis has achieved significant milestones, with yearly emerging cases dipping by 21%, compared to the global decline of 12% between 2015 and 2024. India’s treatment coverage is 92% versus global coverage of 78%. Driven by the intensified TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, cumulative screenings have crossed 28.1 crore, with over 20 lakh individuals provided TB Preventive Treatment (TPT), 5.7 lakh new Nikshay Mitras added, and 46,118 Gram Panchayats awarded TB-free certification. The national response has been substantially accelerated through a 34-fold increase in X-ray screening via handheld units, the rollout of the TB Mukt Bharat App featuring the AI chatbot 'Khushi', and the introduction of the shorter, safer BPaLM (Bedaquiline, Pretomanid, Linezolid, and Moxifloxacin) treatment regimen for drug-resistant patients alongside advanced AI-driven triage tools. Building on this progress, the JOSH (Joint Squad for Health) campaign mobilises young people and communities to promote TB awareness, early detection, timely treatment, and treatment adherence, while addressing stigma. By strengthening community participation and collective action, the campaign reinforces the Jan Andolan approach towards achieving a TB-free India. 




 


 Introduction 


 India is on track towards tuberculosis elimination. New cases of tuberculosis emerging yearly in India have been reduced by 21% from 2015-2024 as compared to the global decline of 12%, according to the World Health Organisation’s Global Tuberculosis Report 2025. India’s treatment coverage is 92% versus global coverage of 78%. 


 


 

 This marks one of the most significant declines in TB incidence globally, exceeding the pace of reduction recorded in other high-burden nations. Deaths due to TB reduced by 28% during the same period. The Government of India’s targeted, multi-pronged approach towards detecting, screening and treating tuberculosis has contributed significantly to this progressive trend. Advanced technology expanded local health services, community engagement, and affordable treatment have put India on track to eliminate this prevalent and potentially fatal disease. 


 


 


 
 JOSH Campaign to Mobilise Communities Towards TB Elimination 


 To further amplify this momentum towards eliminating TB, a nationwide social media campaign featuring JOSH (Joint Squad for Health) Teams – across 11 states and 55 districts on a pilot basis – was organised on 13th October 2026 . Every JOSH team has MY BHARAT volunteers, cadets from the National Cadet Corps, and a designated Class-I officer to spread awareness on timely screening and treatment. 


 This structure mobilises the youth towards grassroots community awareness. All ministries, departments, healthcare institutions, MY Bharat volunteers and youth organisations, students and citizens are encouraged to join in amplifying TB awareness, early detection, treatment adherence and stigma-free communities through posts, photographs, videos and inspiring stories highlighting youth-led action. 


 


 The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare held workshops on the TB Mukt Abhiyaan with members of the Parliament and Legislative Assemblies. However, to take this campaign forward, involving the communities was deemed crucial. The JOSH campaign endeavours to be the next step in increasing community participation , highlighting the importance of screening and early detection. The campaign highlights the requirement for diagnosis and treatment, along with community participation, to increase active screening and to find asymptomatic patients. 


 This community participation and awareness building, particularly in vulnerable and marginalised populations, is crucial for removing fear and increasing awareness in people about treatment and screening as well. Together with the initiative, this campaign is aimed at making TB Mukt Bharat a reality through both institutional support and community mobilisation. 




 


 
 TB and Symptoms 


 What is Tuberculosis? 


 Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by a bacterium called Mycobacterium tuberculosis , usually impacting the lungs. TB can also affect other parts of the body, such as the brain, kidneys, or the spine. 


 A person infected by the bacterium may become sick, but some do not. Inactive TB cases or latent TB infections also exist. People with inactive TB may not spread the disease to others like those with an active TB infection– yet they may develop active TB anytime and become sick. Babies and children, and people with weaker immune systems, are more likely to get sick when infected. Without proper treatment, active TB can be fatal . 


 


 


 TB Symptoms 


 Symptoms of active TB are usually specific to the site affected by the bacteria, though there are some symptoms common to all types of TB. 


 


 People with active or symptomatic TB can spread the TB bacteria to others. When they cough, sneeze or speak, tiny droplets containing the bacteria can be released into the air and inhaled by people nearby—especially in spaces with poor ventilation. 


 Although tuberculosis spreads through the air, it does not transmit through: 


 
 Handshakes 

 Using public toilets 

 Sharing food and utensils 

 Everyday social interactions 

 

 Patients with lung TB generally stop being contagious after they have been on appropriate TB medicines for at least two weeks. People with TB in parts of the body other than the lungs usually cannot spread the disease. 


 


 
 What Should You Do If You Notice Symptoms? 


 The National TB Elimination Programme provides free screening and treatment services across the country at all public health facilities and many private healthcare centres, too. If you or anyone you know is showing TB symptoms: 


 
 Call the toll-free Ni-kshay Sampark TB& Hepatitis helpline: 1800-11-6

 The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), India organised a National Conference on the theme ‘Water as the Elixir of Life: Advancing Human Dignity through the Right to Water’ at Vigyan Bhawan, New Delhi today, as part of the celebrations marking its 33rd Foundation Day. The Conference brought together representatives of government institutions, development organisations and other stakeholders to deliberate on the human rights dimensions of access to safe drinking water, sustainable management of water resources, rejuvenation of water bodies, community participation and the need to strengthen institutional mechanisms for ensuring water security. 


 


 Addressing the first session on ‘Water conservation, sustainability and community participation’ Shri Brijendra Swaroop, Executive Director (Projects), National Mission for Clean Ganga, Ministry of Jal Shakti emphasised that non-discriminatory access to adequate, safe and affordable water is fundamental to human dignity. Outlining the Namami Gange Programme, he highlighted its Integrated River Basin Management approach and the objectives of ensuring Nirmal Dhara (unpolluted flow), Aviral Dhara (continuous flow) and protection of the Ganga’s geological and ecological integrity. The programme comprises 527 projects with a sanctioned cost of approximately Rs 43,326 crore, covering pollution abatement, ecological restoration, biodiversity conservation, community participation, research and livelihood enhancement. 


 He stressed the need for comprehensive wastewater management, maintenance of ecological flows, protection of floodplains, wetland restoration and biodiversity conservation. Referring to improvements in water quality in several stretches of the Ganga, he observed that the success of rejuvenation efforts should be assessed through environmental outcomes, including water quality, biodiversity and ecosystem functioning, rather than expenditure or the number of completed projects alone. He called for scientific mapping of water bodies, catchment-based planning, institutional convergence and community participation, emphasising that conservation must precede restoration. 


 


 Shri Yugal Kishore Joshi, Programme Director, NITI Aayog highlighted India’s water-security challenges, noting that the country has approximately 4% of the world’s freshwater resources but nearly 18% of its population. Per capita water availability has declined to approximately 1,300–1,400 cubic metres annually, below the water-stress threshold of 1,700 cubic metres. He emphasised integrating traditional water-harvesting practices with modern scientific methods, strengthening Gram Panchayats, preparing water budgets and addressing encroachment. 


 Citing a community-led initiative covering approximately 800 villages, in which water-body rejuvenation had been completed in 731 villages at an approximate cost of Rs. 3 lakh per water body, he highlighted the importance of community labour and productive use of excavated silt. He called for stronger local institutions, improved monitoring and wider replication of successful conservation initiatives. 


 Ms.Anjali Makhija, CEO and Trustee, S M Sehgal Foundation highlighted the importance of collaboration among communities, government, development organisations, academia and other stakeholders in addressing water and agricultural challenges. She outlined the Foundation’s work on groundwater recharge, supplementary surface-water storage, rainwater harvesting in schools, water quality and climate-smart, water-efficient agriculture, including drip and sprinkler irrigation and laser land levelling. 


 She emphasised the role of women’s groups and village development committees in identifying priorities, contributing resources and maintaining water structures. Stressing the need to work in coordination with local and district administrations, she advocated combining traditional knowledge with scientific expertise through GIS mapping, soil-moisture and water-quality monitoring as well as third-party assessments. She also called for affordable and accessible technology, greater philanthropic and CSR investment in water and agriculture, besides the development of a scientifically designed water-credit system.

Emphasising that knowledge and advocacy must translate into meaningful environmental action, he called for drawing upon traditional wisdom to conserve natural resources, restore rivers and preserve ecological balance for future generations.

 The Ministry of Information & Broadcasting has launched Special Campaign 6.0 from 2nd October 2026, with 610 of its offices across the country participating in the campaign. The campaign aims to enhance cleanliness in government offices and reduce pendency. Emphasis is also being laid on the effective collection, segregation and disposal of e-waste. 


 During the Preparatory Phase, all Media Units, along with their field formations, including the Main Secretariat, were directed to finalise targets, identify pending references and plan for space management. 


 Union Minister for Information & Broadcasting, Railways and Electronics & IT, Shri Ashwini Vaishnaw, interacted with senior officers of the Ministry and Media Units during the Preparatory Phase. He urged all concerned to cover every office, down to the lowest unit of the Ministry, and instructed that the campaign should continue beyond 31st October 2026 and become a year-round drive. Public dealing offices are to be given high priority, and good work needs to be publicised through various social media platforms. 


 Secretary (I&B), Shri Chanchal Kumar, reviewed the preparations for and implementation of the campaign with all Heads of Media Units and their Nodal Officers. He issued directions for taking appropriate and timely action to achieve the targets set for this year's campaign. 


 The Ministry has performed well in previous Special Campaigns, demonstrating a consistent commitment to institutionalising Swachhata and ensuring the timely disposal of pending matters.  Union Minister of State for Power and New & Renewable Energy, Shri Shripad Yesso Naik, represented India at the 20th East Asia Summit Energy Ministers’ Meeting held in Manila, Philippines, today. Addressing the Meeting, Shri Naik emphasised India’s commitment to strengthening regional energy cooperation, energy security and a secure, resilient, affordable and sustainable energy future. 


 


 Underscoring India’s Act East Policy and its Comprehensive Strategic Partnership with ASEAN, the Minister welcomed the ASEAN Plan of Action for Energy Cooperation 2026–2030 and stressed cooperation under the ASEAN India Plan of Action 2026–2030, including the ASEAN Power Grid, regional power transmission, multilateral power trade, clean energy and energy security. He also recalled Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s announcement at the 22nd ASEAN India Summit in 2025 to support the ASEAN Power Grid initiative through training of 400 professionals on grid connectivity. 


 


 Shri Naik drew attention to India’s significant progress in the power sector, with installed electricity generation capacity reaching 558.8 GW as on 30 th September, 2026, including 308 GW of non fossil capacity, accounting for 55% of total installed capacity. He also highlighted the progress under PM Surya Ghar, with approximately 5.01 million rooftop solar installations benefiting 5.95 million households as on September 29, 2026. He noted that India had achieved 50 per cent of cumulative installed electricity generation capacity from non fossil sources in June 2025, five years ahead of its 2030 NDC target. 


 On regional interconnection, Shri Naik stated that India and Singapore are exploring options for a proposed 2,000 MW cross border power interconnection. One option under consideration is a land based transmission corridor of approximately 3,000 km connecting Imphal in India to Singapore through Myanmar, Thailand and Malaysia. The proposed interconnection has the potential to facilitate reliable cross border electricity trade, support clean energy integration and strengthen regional energy security. 


 The Minister expressed India’s readiness to share its experience in large scale renewable energy deployment, grid integration, transmission planning, energy storage, green hydrogen and clean energy technologies with EAS participating countries. He also called for greater institutional linkages between the ASEAN Centre for Energy and Indian institutions including NTPC, POWERGRID, CEA, NIWE, NISE and NPTI. 


 Shri Naik further outlined opportunities for cooperation on strategic petroleum reserves, emergency preparedness, electricity system resilience, LNG and gas supply security, renewable energy forecasting, battery energy storage, green hydrogen and other emerging energy technologies. He also expressed India’s interest in knowledge exchange and cooperation with ASEAN partners on CCUS and Carbon Credit Trading Scheme, taking into account the priorities and circumstances of participating countries. 


 He reaffirmed India’s support for ASEAN’s efforts to operationalise the Enhanced Memorandum of Understanding on the ASEAN Power Grid and deepen multilateral power trade.
